A lightly interactive storytelling presentation where you're the surveillance state, combing through people's files and conversations... but then uh-oh! get this! what if the surveillance state ISN'T A GOOD THING? Gosh! 

"Papers, Please" seems to be the aspiration here. Well, that game manages to pull off something affecting because 1) it has an actual gameplay component that cleverly creates tension with the ethics, and 2) its writing is terse and flavorful and very carefully styled. Orwell is 0 for 2.

Basically, the piece as a whole is exactly as literate and well-considered and native-English-speaking as its title: "Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You." If you think that title sounds cool, you might well find this a compelling experience; clearly many people do. But if you're raising an eyebrow at it, I encourage you to just trust your gut and move along.

GENERAL OVERVIEW
Awesome game and "out-of-the-box" genre. Gameplay is very interesting since you analyze the suspects from a digital device, without physically following them. You get to know every small aspects of their lives, but this is a factor that greatly complicates the developer's work. For the ones who love the detective genre, this one is a very good choice. But I can't give a fully positive opinion on this: let's start with the upsides.
PROS
1)Rich and deep story. Keeps the gamer interested.
2)Orwell system is very well structured, its display is simple and not effort-requiring.
3)Plot-twists excluded, the game is actually chill. It keeps you concentrated, but not nervous or stressed. The fact that you can sit down and think of your next move, gives the game the right pace.
CONS
1)Low graphic and audio impact. Although the story keeps the gamer focused, that is probably the only one factor. I dare to say the game has a poor multimedial content. Characters don't "say" a single word for all the story.. You just hear music and other minor sound effects.
2)Too often it remains unclear where "the game finishes and the gamer starts". Has it ever happened to you that you can't understand how heavy will your decision be on your remaining gameplay? It happens too many times in Orwell. It's not clear when your action will bring to irreversible consequences, and this is annoying. Sometimes it feels like the game is playing you, and this is boring because the plot does not prompt the player to take important actions.
3)Insufficiently exhaustive tutorial. Although Orwell is pretty much a game with a "simple dynamic", basically gathering relevant information, I think that the small tutorial in the beginning does not clarify enough what the Orwell system is about. Even though in the tutorial-phase of the game is explained how you should deal with Orwell, the gamer fully grasps the concept after some time, and this is not acceptable in a game where choices matter (especially in one where it's not clear where choices are supposed to be made!). I came from hundreds of detective-genre games but this one is different, the developer knows, so maybe they should have stressed the basic principle more.
4)Lack of languages. This is a text-adventure. There should be plenty of available languages! I understand that this would be an incredibly long job... But this is a noticeable downside. This is quite a problem for non-natives english speakers, and a barrier for non english speakers.
5) You gather information on this system called Orwell, but as you go on with the game, you may find out more precise details, or that the information you considered relevant are just circumstancial. This is a normal day in the life of an investigator. So, why can't the player modify the datachunks relating to characters' pages? this is a forcing. A super complex system like Orwell doesn't allow the investigator to cancel what he wrote?
OVERALL OPINION
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a very nice game, that will be appreciated by most of the detective-games community. It's passionating, you would never desire it to end, it makes you feel a real investigator. Nevertheless, it has noteworthy downsides and there's a wide improvement margin under some aspects. Recommended.

[h1] Internet voyeurism in the name of public safety [/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] is an unconventional, surprisingly open-ended game about performing surveillance work on the Internet in the name of safety and anti-terrorism measures. 

As a newly appointed surveillance worker, you are to investigate a newly committed terror bombing. Who did it? Why? Does the culprit belong to a larger cluster of terrorists? Will it happen again? As you investigate, various suspects will emerge. You find out about their existence through good old-fashioned online stalking: social media, email accounts, and private chats are all fair play. Their past, their personalities, and their interconnections become increasingly clear, and the online posts gradually deepen into surprisingly convincing pictures of real human beings, with real lives, who are subject to real integrity violations. They may be guilty, or they may not. You, however, most certainly are; rummaging through every embarassing forum post, every private email, and every delicious piece of browser history for your superiors to harvest. After all: your employers are morally perfect people, who can be trusted with this information. Right? 

Game mechanically, [i]Orwell[/i] plays like a text-based point-and-click puzzler featuring source criticism. You will often simply drag and drop information highlighted to you. In these cases, the game feels like story-based pixel hunting. Occasionally, there is misleading information: quotes out of context should not be taken as gospel, nor should outright lies. Every now and then, sources contradict one another. It is then up to you to decide who to trust.  This game flow continues unimpeded for most of the game, eventually growing slightly stale and mindless before some lategame twists shake things up. Progression went smoothly most of the time. The only bottlenecks were the few times a single, specific piece of information was needed to move on, sending me backtracking for details I had missed.

There are various [i]1984[/i] references, and the entire game is essentially Orwellian themes translated to a 21st Century surveillance society. The idea of reluctantly serving a tyrannical regime is here, although lighter. So is the fear of punishment for having the wrong sympathies. Again, this paranoia is more impactful in the novel, but not without merit here either. Although [i]Orwell[/i] never reaches the same psychological detail as the novel (understandable, given its 5-hour runtime), it works as a re-tread of these themes. The difference is the packaging: the surveillance is no longer camera-based, but has moved to the Internet accounts and hardware of the modern era... like my Steam account, and the PC used for this review.

The game makes a point about our own responsibilities; about how the cog in the surveillance machine has a will of its own. The difference is that here, the point is made interactively. In doing so, [i]Orwell[/i] becomes reminiscent not only of [i]1984[/i], but of [i] Paper's Please[/i] as well. That game, too, raises the question of whether "just having followed orders" is sufficient to escape moral responsibility. Indeed, [i] Paper's Please[/i], and [i]Orwell [/i] are both graphically simple games, with simple puzzle gameplay and complicated social issues side by side.  

Posting this review makes me slightly uncomfortable. I am wary of the data I upload to the Internet. This review is part of my digital fingerprint. A piece of me, my tastes, my way of expression, and my experiences are now up there for anyone to see. I hope you enjoyed the access.

A dire and very timely warning, the game takes places in a fictional country where the government is adopting more and more authoritarian and - well, Orwellian - methods of surveillance and control. You're recruited by the eponymous government agency that is in charge of combating crime, and your handling of emerging evidence determines if you contribute to the country's descent into a police state or not.  

I liked the premise, but I found it all a bit too caricatured, although the game switches things up by presenting an alternate contemporary reality where the authoritarian push comes from the other side. 

Most of all, I was disappointed that the game puts a prominent highlight on every relevant piece of information you come across. Not only that, you even get direct notifications for cross-referenced sources, so basically you don't even have to read and remember anything. Sure, you make some interesting (but as I said, also pretty obvious) decisions about what to do with the tidbits, but it would be so much more fun and engaging if you actually had to identify the relevant puzzle pieces on your own. 

Maybe these mechanics are just there for the sake of convenience, but ultimately they make the sleuthing trivial, and that's a problem when combing through news/websites/chats *is* the gameplay.

As a game, it's way too scripted and practically visual novel -like, allowing practically no freedom of action for the player in what is presented as an interactive plot system.

Orwell does present a good criticism of government security and crime-fighting total surveillance programs that have been popping up around the world for at least the last decade. The story highlights many of the fundamental issues with such programs. It's just a pity that the story experience is ruined by the restrictive gameplay system, that forces you to do things in a silly way and backtrack to earlier data sources to use data blocks only later unlocked..

A key plot device element that got totally overlooked in the game design is that an attentive player could turn the use of the Orwell system on its head quite early on significantly affecting the story outcome to fit the canon narrative, but this is simply not possible in the game.

Oh dear, oh dear - what a disappointment. I had high hopes for this, but it essentially proved to be a pretty linear story in to which you fit, with some variations. Steam says I've played for four hours, which is enough for 1.5 play through and to see that my actions have, by and large, very little effect on the outcome of the game.

Now, some people like this sort of game - the sort of people who thought Telltale games were amazing. I don't. I guess I wouldn't mind if it was a big story, but tbh it's over pretty quick. 

So, gameplay - pretty weak. Longevity, dreadful - I won't bother coming back to this. Sure, I know I can tweak the outcomes a little, but ultimately it doesn't really matter.

Now for the concept - some people reviewing this have described as some kind of clever, deep warning about the state and it's Orwellian nature. Ok, this isn't a new concept and there are other games that do it better - more to the point - there are other films that do it better (some based on Orwell's own work). I found this a blunt effort to make a point that is pretty obvious to most of us. Maybe that's what people like, I don't. I prefer a little subtlety - not being slapped in the face by the concept every few seconds. 

So, in short. This could have been a great game, if either the library of stories was bigger or the player could have more impact on the outcome. The positives? Well the user interface works fairly well, although there is a lot of repeat clicking and the bookmark system doesn't seem to work desperately well - those are minor complaints though. Graphically, it looks ok - there just isn't much substance to back it up. I'm glad I waited for it to be on sale.

An interesting game. It emulates well how someone can be in the middle of an investigation while not being there at all/invisible to all.

The gameplay in itself is pretty straightforward. Scoop through the internet (webpages, blogs, bank statements,etc) or phone chat/call history for specific chunks of data pertaining to your investigation case. Information you find of relevance can be uploaded to the "system" to then be used. Be careful however which information you upload as you can't take the data back. It might not be very clear in the early game but you are a drone worker and not a decision maker and the people evaluating your data will take it in the strictest sense. You have to lead your investigator to the correct conclusions by "filtering" the data you transmit. Something that I didn't do at all in my first playthrough (which is not over yet). 

Once I'll have finished the first I'll definitely start a second one to see if I can avert some unwanted consequences.
